I gave the client a good amount of headroom, probably too much.  The headroom is the following:

Vanilla system:
Requirement 1 - The player must be in water or lava
Requirement 2 - The player must have X movement, Y movement + 0.6, Z movement bounding box area no collision
Requirement 3 - The player must have horizontal collision

My implementation:
Requirement 1 - The player must be within 0.1 blocks of water or lava
Requirement 2 - The player must have X movement, Y movement + 0.6, Z movement bounding box minus 0.1 blocks have no collision
Requirement 3 - The player must have something to collide with within 0.1 blocks

At most cheaters could bob on top of water by the shore.  This doesn't matter because swimming is faster anyways.  You don't get an advantage by bobbing on top of the water by the shore about 10% faster than everyone else.

Yeah, I've confirmed and this is a bug in vanilla.  Fireworks can tick both at the beginning or the end of the tick.  Hell, a firework could tick twice doubling it's effect while not ticking at all for the next tick.  This completely breaks the lag compensation for fireworks boosting the player, and explains why the lag compensation is going so badly.

Here is the first possible solution that I can think of
Vector 1: All possible fireworks on the past look vector
Vector 2: All possible fireworks on the next look vector

If the vector is in between these, the player's movement is legit

However, there is a possibility that the possible aren't ran between player ticks at all and are ran twice on the next tick relative to the player, so here is the next solution:
Vector 1: All possible fireworks * 2 on the past look vector
Vector 2: All possible fireworks * 2 on the next look vector
Vector 3: No fireworks at all

I don't believe it is feasible or performance efficient to try and find how many fireworks each player exactly used.  I guess the check could just use the player's ping to try and lag compensate fireworks activating, instead of the current solution calculating the number of fireworks being used.  This is just really complicated and I think the best solution might just be to get "close enough" to the possible valid movement.  I can calcuate ping by the first firework +- 25 ms

I'm not having any issue with going from input -> output, but output -> input is difficult when fireworks are buggy.

One possible issue is a cheat simply doubling the effect of fireworks on the player, but it really isn't too big of a deal since multiple fireworks aren't THAT much faster than one firework, it's by like 0.01 which makes be doubt any cheat dev will actually do that.

I guess I'll just use this compromise until client devs try and create an elytra cheat to double the number of fireworks executed, giving a very slight advantage that really doesn't matter at all.  It's a good compromise to allow better "precision" to stop other more important elytra cheats.

Thread safe implementation
- Mark the last transaction packet sent to the client on netty thread
- On velocity send, get the last transaction packet send and add velocity packet into a list on a hashmap
- Mark the last transaction packet received from the client
- On movement packet, mark the last transaction packet that we have gotten


Possible velocities are from the last transaction + 1 from the last movement packet to the current transaction.  The player must take at least one knockback from this list, otherwise they have 100% antikb.


This should be 100% accurate and 100% thread safe.  Sending 10 velocity packets to the client in a tick might affect performance of the anticheat, but even with max qdisc/clumsy settings it mathematically shouldn't be able to break the anticheat.


Possible exploits is messing with the transaction packets to combine velocities so that the player only has to take one knockback.  A possible check could be comparing movement packet jitter versus transaction jitter.  Somewhat difficult as combining knockbacks with enough lag is a vanilla feature.

Fix: Mark transaction packet sent before, put value on HashMap<Short, Boolean>.  The player is flying if the received current transaction ID is greater than or equal to (or overflowed to) the value where it was sent.  Loop values from the last movement packet to the current one and remove them from the HashMap, similar to proposed velocity implementation.  Last value is applied of course.

- Note the last transaction packet sent on a movement packet

Movement packet has the following latency:
- client -> server

One funny solution is just running all 9 inputs, but that doesn't solve when stuff is less than 0.03.  Another solution is the following:

- Check for blocks within 0.05 horizontal of the player
- Run the inputs for colliding against the blocks
- Replace the ladder and the water hopping code with the results from these inputs.


What this accomplishes:
- Reduce threat of bypasses from the ladder and swim hop velocities, as valid inputs are ran

What this fails at:
- More lag
- More memory usage to store past things


How to real-time protect:
- We need to check for collisions within 0.05 blocks of the player and set it to a boolean
- We need to store the velocities of two ticks ago
- If the current tick does not line up, rewind time and use new inputs in the direction against the wall.


I don't like this new solution, but I like the current solution less.

Best solution is to resend players blocks 8x8x8 blocks around the player when they are getting violations that look like ghost blocks.

For blocks that are there on the server but not the client

One way to do it is the Verus/Kauri way, checking if the player's y is on a multiple of 0.015625.

Problems with this way:
- We are open source, cheat makers will just make everything look like a ghost block


Another way is to make a list of all the changed blocks in the player's chunk cache.

To do this, we need 65536 bits per chunk, or 8.192 KiB.

If a player is getting excessive violations that look like a ghost block, such as trying to move into a block, resend chunks.  If a player continues, punish them.  We have a chunk cache so doing this won't slow down the server.

Problems with this way:
- It tells the user to stop cheating, so we might lose cheaters by doing this
- The chunk cache MIGHT be a tick off for block breaking/placing, although it shouldn't be.

Block predictions:
- When the client starts to destroy a block, instabreaks, finishes breaks a block, use item, or use item on, the client sends the server an acknowledgement packet.
- When the player is predicting and sets a block it stores the changed block into a list

Server confirmations:
- Server verified states are changed with the block change and multi block change packets
- After a the server gets the prediction sequence, it sends changed blocks to the client and the sequence ID.  The client then removes local block changes up to that point

Bugs:
- Resending entire chunks, although likely not supported, will break this
- Pistons will create ghost blocks, still
- ViaVersion, in tradition, fucks up this translation and will create flickering blocks on 1.19+

* Mojang kept some quite stupid block changes that were previously added to fix what was done with sequence ID... this means that outdated clients still work fine on 1.19+ servers, it just wastes a bit of bandwidth

Indeed, after closer inspection this was caused by ViaFabric 1.19.1/2 setting on 1.19.4 client, closing.

This issue stems from the fact that when you hit an entity, attack slowdown can be applied. At this time it also calls `this.setSprinting(false);`. But this change never gets sent, because sprint can get reset back to true and the sprint packet is only sent when it changes...

The setSprinting method itself also resets the sprinting attribute, meaning that the client will get rid of any sprinting modifier set by the server. 

I've been experimenting with a "fix" that, when the player attacks an entity and was sprinting and they didn't send a new sprint packet, does the following:
- Receives a packet (silently) to the server that toggles sprint
- Resets the player's sprinting attribute, like the client would have done

It seems to work quite well, but it's not a perfect fix (and it breaks how sprinting normally behaves on hitting entities).

> detecting backtrack in an open source anticheat is kind of useless (easy to bypass since u know what and how it checks)
backtrack basically is achieved by delaying incoming packets, so clientside your hitting an entity at an old position (reach < 3) which results in that reachy hit since serverside hes already out of those 3 blocks

> in theory mitigating backtrack doesnt need to be mitigated with high ping 
ppl could just listen on positionupdate and check if the last transaction received is longer than x and increase a buffer

it would fail for someone who is currently downloading anything since having lower downloading speed will eventually increase the time when client receives a packet (== incoming delay) 

what could be done is some kind of accuracy check which checks if the players only delays incoming when in theory it would give him an advantage (basically checking lag in relation to the distance to his opponent)

> Can this be used to improve the Reach check?

Right clicking outside of the hitbox flags Reach and BadPacketsT if you have hitbox enabled;
Right clicking an entity regardless of where you interacted with it will consistently flag BadPacketsT (as long as you're sending the packet) if you have hitbox enabled.

Therefore, it don't think it can be seen as an improvement for the Reach check as the player doesn't necessarily have to hit/interact outside of the hitbox, however, I've seen other anticheats where this check is called "Hitbox", "HitboxB" or "ReachB". Excluding it won't work because `discord-webhooks` depends on `okio` which is written in Kotlin. Downgrading `discord-webhooks` was chosen over relocating the `kotlin` package because `kotlin-stdlib` makes the jar 2 MB larger, which was the reason MWHunter downgraded it a year ago: 6094a700fcc9e9de9cdaea433470c006a32a77cd
This is why it's a terrible idea to write libraries in Kotlin - bad interpolation with Java projects and adds required Kotlin libraries.

For reference, I will list all these issues with flying:

- Clients such as Lunar have built-in flying cheats
- Mojangs netcode is very broken with flying
- The client will tick its movement, it then checks 1) The player is on the ground, 2) They are flying, 3) They are not in spectator. If this is the case, flying is set to false and an abilities update is sent
- But this means we don't see the hidden flying movement, as we believe it to be false, because movement packets are sent after this new status. This is what causes this specific landing issue.
- The player can hold jump under a block whilst flying and this will increase velocity, however this increase in velocity is invisible to the server
- Spectator mode has a hidden feature where scrolling can change the client-side fly speed

2) the plugin is obfuscated. This is because Class.forName("ac.grim.grimac.shaded.teleportation.FoliaTeleporter") is called and strings like this will not match the obfuscated class names. When this errors, Bukkit.getServer().getPluginManager().disablePlugin(plugin) is called

Additionally, the use of a separate module is unnecessary. Java doesn't care if code is calling methods that don't exist at runtime until it is actually used, so we can actually just wrap the folia specific call behind FoliaScheduler.isFolia() so that it is never ran unless the server would actually have this method. If it isn't folia, just call the usual method.

finally, this entire PR can be replaced by just calling PaperLib.teleportAsync(entity, location) as we don't need sync teleports for spectating. PaperLib works fine on spigot, paper, and folia and is the proper way to accomplish this.

This check has now been extensively overhauled and is ready for review before being merged.

A summary of the changes:
- Added a new check called LineOfSightPlace, that primarily raytraces the player's position PostFlyingBlockPlace (when we have accurate information about the player's rotation) to see if placing a block is possible or is blocked by another block.
  - This check covers a few cases of entities blocking rays, but is not intended to and does not completely do so.
  - This check is latency compensated and accounts for all possible player lookdirs and eye heights.
  - This check accounts for the different hitboxes of blocks in Minceraft
  - This check accounts for 0.03/0.0002
- Removed RotationPlace, since LineOfSightPlace supersedes it in terms of functionalty. It is RotationPlace if it checked for walls inbetween.
- In addition, it is possible (disabled by default) to make this check only run against a block whitelist to save reduce the performance impact. This is primarily intended for server owners who want to block illegal access to containers.

Notes:
- This check in its current state merges in @SamB440's changes to the reach check, since the functionality was very similar and there is shared code. Sam's Reach checks remain experimental since they do not account for 0.03/0.0002 and are _disabled by default_ unlike the LineOfSightPlace check, which does account for this behaviour and has been tested by myself extensively.

Potential Future TODOs:
- Figure out a way to cancel a block placement postFly.
- Flag & block mining/block breaking that fails to meet these checks
- Detect if entity is blocking placement of a bloc.

## We Have an 0.03/0.002 Problem - Fixing it Creates Another Problem
### Background
For those who don't know, as I discovered when writing this check, Minecraft clients do not send their location to the server unless they have moved more than 0.03 blocks. Since 1.18.2 it is now 0.0002 blocks. This means to compensate for potential falses we need to account for the player's position being up to 0.03/0.002 blocks off. For my check, that means expanding hitboxes.

### What I Did & I Didn't Do This Before
To account for this 0.03/0.002 issues, we increase the hitbox of the target block by 0.03/0.002 depending on the player version. In theory we also should decrease the size of the hitboxes of every other block we trace that is not the target block by 0.03/0.002. 

The problem is the naive way of doing this leaves a bypass that for < 1.18.2 players is fairly exploitable. Simply look at the edges of a full block and freecam through to open a chest on the other side. So long as your looking at ~0.03 from the edge of the block you will not be detected. It is tedious, more difficult to do, and placing blocks behind whiles becomes harder with this check but not impossible.

In my testing in 1.21 I've been unable to false after cumulatively playing for days, so I decided to leave it out, as I was designing this for myself and modern versions of the game.

### What can be done?
As far as I'm aware of, we basically have 3 options here.

1. Apply 0.03/0.002 adjustments to non-target blocks for players 
  - Make both a config option with 0.03 on by default and 0.002 off by default.
    - We want 0.002 off by default because it is small enough I've yet to realistically false flag, and I don't want to create an 0.004 long gap at the edges between the hitboxes of two blocks that player's can bypass through for servers that only support modern versions.
2. Come up with a way to bake meshes (combine hitboxes of adjacent/connected blocks) in realtime for blocks within the FOV of the player except the target block and shrink that mesh by 0.03/0.002. 
  - This will prevent gaps from forming between block hitboxes allowing players to bypass by looking at edges **completely**
  - Performance hit is probably not gonna look great. I suppose we'll have to test then try but my intuition tells me that to do this at scale and in realtime you might need a GPU with mesh shader support (AMD RX 6XXX+, NVIDIA RTX 20XX+, Intel ARC) installed on the server.
  - A pretty good solution for mini-game maps where we can precompute most of the work and where the map doesn't change because no blocks are placed/broken. Doors, trapdoors, and other blocks that change on interaction can either be ignored or handled as edge cases.
  3. Get a really accurate picture of when a player is moving and only apply 0.03/0.002 adjustments for non-target blocks when the player is standing still or moving < x blocks per second. 
  - This will reduce the false rate by a few orders or magnitude at minimum and the difficulty of exploiting the hole produced by 0.03/0.002 is increased significantly.

The only "cheating" behavior here I see is breaking the door from too far away. We should catch this with FarBreak/RotationBreak/PositionBreak checks. Moving through blocks that don't exist on the client is legitimate. During testing, I found out that this also works when breaking the blocks and using Blink instead of Freecam so the blocks aren't being replaced, so there would still be a way to bypass this even with break checks. In my opinion, there are only two ways to patch this:

1. Setback (don't flag) when moving into/through blocks that exist on the server but not on the client. This will patch the issue but might make combat that involves the opponent placing blocks less enjoyable for high ping players because the setbacks might not be exactly like the vanilla ones which will occur in high ping block placement combat. Some other anticheats also do this.

How do people feel about using my existing Vector implementation (yes I know its slow, it's more about the interfaces and how it works)? Is everyone fine with using the factory to create new instances and static imports?

I know I could probably speed it up just a little by eliminating the casting but that would require treating people on scalar as Second class citizens. 

I figured it would be worth it since people still run Xeon V1/V2s for Minecraft servers and the oldest machines with support for AVX-256 for doubles are Haswell chips from 2013 (Intel Core i7-4770K & Intel Xeon E5-2697 v3)

Key differences below: (rest are mostly just replacing existing usage of Bukkit Vectors)
- https://github.com/GrimAnticheat/Grim/pull/1841/files#diff-9d977bf910697b7ece45500d0365d3c4cf6cb5e9b7f95475e210380a01e42862

EDIT: This would likely supersede https://github.com/GrimAnticheat/Grim/pull/1765

It seems Project Panama has abandoned allowing you to ignore safety for performance by directly calling a method with its memory address in Java 21 which somewhat embarrassingly means that all of the implementations here (with the exception of SIMD cross product on Project Panama) will probably be slower than Scalar unless we batch them. The overhead is just too high when you're doing operations that are measured in nanoseconds.

I'll probably write a NalimVector3D implementation later just to prove we can beat the JVM if we try hard enough when I have time and post benchmarks later.

You could try disabling https://github.com/GrimAnticheat/Grim/blob/2.0/src/main/java/ac/grim/grimac/manager/SetbackTeleportUtil.java#L358, note that this will expose your server to disabler exploits.

```
Benchmark                                      Mode  Cnt   Score    Error  Units
NalimVector3DBenchmark.benchmarkCrossProduct   avgt    3   5.622 ±  0.409  ns/op
SIMDVector3DBenchmark.benchmarkCrossProduct    avgt    3  19.063 ± 57.292  ns/op
ScalarVector3DBenchmark.benchmarkCrossProduct  avgt    3   5.466 ±  1.033  ns/op
```
As you can see for very simple/trivial functions like these the overhead of using these techniques is often not worth it. Even using Nalim with SIMD the cost of calling the C function is too high. For vectors batching is needed for it to be worth it.

In any case. This is not important; the goal of this draft is too add the right tooling to the project to take advantage of SIMD, and low overhead native code calls. I'll continue to update this draft with example code and project setup to make it easy to understand how to take advantage of these features for real performance gains.

I don't have a clear picture as to how mounting/dismounting vehicles works pre 1.21.4 because I never looked into it, but I will describe precisely how it works in 1.21.4 and you can see if there are any discrepancies/new stuff 


SERVER:
Leaving boats appears to be server-side, in player rideTick(), the server checks player.wantsToStopRiding() which simply checks

isShiftKeyDown()
 (isShiftKeyDown is controlled by the client in 2 ways, when they send ServerboundPlayerCommandPacket with either press shift key or release shift key actions and they can change whether their shift key is down inside of ServerboundInteractPacket isUsingSecondaryAction() flag, grim already has all of this logic covered)
 
 it then triggers stopRiding() which calls 
 
 removeVehicle() which removes the entities vehicle reference, and removes the entity from the vehicles passenger list.
 
 then it runs dismountVehicle() for the entity, which finds a free position to place the player nearby and calls teleportTo() with said position, this calls setPosRaw() which as the name suggests sets the entities position values, yaw and pitch, not informing the client in any way.
 
At this point in time, the client should still be on the vehicle sneaking, at the same position, because the server has yet to tell them anything

remember removeVehicle() from earlier though? the server ticks the entity tracker newTrackerTick() before it ticks entities, so in the tick AFTER stopRiding(), sendChanges() is called on the vehicle entity by the tracker which checks if the passenger list has changed, which it was the previous tick, this causes it to send a ClientboundSetPassengersPacket to the client, and finally it sends a ClientboundPlayerPositionPacket to the player passenger informing them of their current server-side x y and z, here is the logic for sending that ClientboundPlayerPositionPacket packet:
 
 
Side note, the x y and z we are about to inform them about always be the same exact position as what we set it to last tick, as packet processing for the last tick happened before rideTick() and packet processing for the current tick happens after the entity tracker tick we are currently in. Just in case you thought the player might be able to move during the tick gap between removing passengers and sending the update packet
 
teleport() is called which runs some bukkit event logic, unimportant for now, then it calls 
internalTeleport() which sets justTeleported flag to true, unimportant,
it will also set a timestamp of the current tick called awaitingTeleportTime,
and it will set the players raw pos again to the teleport position, as it may have been changed by the bukkit teleport event.
It will then set a variable in the player awaitingPositionFromClient to the target teleport location, in this case still the dismount point location. 
It will then finally dispatches the ClientboundPlayerPositionPacket to the client.
This ClientboundPlayerPositionPacket contains the position of the player on the server (obviously) but also includes another field which is incremented called awaitingTeleport, basically a transaction ID, this will be important later

Remember that awaitingPositionFromClient field? its logic is important, while the client has this field set they are in "pending teleport" state
- their ServerboundUseItemOnPacket packets are ignored
- their ServerboundMoveVehiclePacket packets are ignored
- their ServerboundMovePlayerPacket packets are ignored

if awaitingTeleportTime exceeds 20 ticks while in pending teleport state, i.e we haven't gotten back a response to the teleport from the client (ServerboundAcceptTeleportationPacket) in over a second, teleport() will be re-ran basically telling them again "this is your position" this logic is disabled on paper however, as for clients with over 1000ms ping, this creates a buggy experience.

lol another side note, issue found in paper while reviewing code, awaitingPositionFromClient redundantly checked twice https://github.com/PaperMC/Paper/issues/11895
 
 
CLIENT:
Now we are on the client side, the client receives a ClientboundSetPassengersPacket packet which causes it to stopRiding() for all passengers to sync it with the server state.
ClientboundPlayerPositionPacket when recieved by the client will first check if the player is a passenger of any sorts, which will return false because setpassengerspacket is sent first and it removed the player as a passenger.
it will then call setValuesFromPositionPacket() which sets the clients posraw in the exact same way as the server did earlier, finally we are in sync, the player finally sends a ServerboundAcceptTeleportationPacket with the transaction ID from earlier back to the server and it also sends a ServerboundMovePlayerPacket with the players current client updated position and yaw 

SERVER:
If the transaction ID sent back from the client matches the awaitingTeleport, the server will once again set the raw pos to awaitingPositionFromClient, seemingly redundantly though because I don't know how their position could have changed but better safe than sorry I guess, and as for that serverboundmoveplayerpacket the player sends, there is no extra special handling, theoretically the player should appear to have moved 0 distance.

> do you ever set expandNonRelative to false?

No. The `newPacketLocation` ReachInterpolationData object becomes `oldPacketLocation` when we receive a transaction (see the onFirstTransaction method). 

`newPacketLocation` is replaced by a new instance of ReachInterpolationData that has expandNonRelative set to false. `oldPacketLocation` then becomes the next `newPacketLocation` and is cleared by GC.

This means that when a ReachInterpolationData instance is expanded its never shrunk again, but this is fine since we replace it when we receive the next couple transactions with non-expanded instances.

It you trace all possible iterations of this code, this is impossible. 

> I looked and I only see this method being called from a single thread so I don't understand how it's throwing a CME

addRealTimeTask() executes runnables outside of the synchronized block. Its possible for another thread to call addRealTimeTask() and run a runnable on another thread that modifies the transactionMap or finishes executing after the lock has released in another thread or part of the code.

If you get really unlucky and modify transactionMap while its being iterated over in handleNettySyncTransaction() you can get a CME.

> could using a `ConcurrentLinkedDeque` instead of a `LinkedList` fix this?

As I mentioned in my PR description:
> * Chose not to use a ConcurrnetLinkedQueue because iteration may not reflect state of data structure and working to ensure this is always correct for our use case was too complicated


ConcurrentLinkedQueue isn't magic unfortunately, its possible for iteration of the data structure to not reflect its underlying state which could lead to subtle bugs. For example if a runnable deletes an item in the list (not head or tail) it could lead to iteration skipping some runnables. Even if our own code doesn't do this we have no guarantee when we open up Grim with the check API that other checks won't trigger these issues (and that is something I'm unsure about).

CopyOnWriteArrayList or some variant of it *might* be what we're looking for but that would be even slower than what I'm already doing.

> Transactions are sent before flying, so we would reset the variable before we receive the new rotation, I don’t think this is the correct way to fix this

Yes, the order per client tick is transactions, attacks/interacts, then flying, right?

- The horseInteractCausedForcedRotation is set to true on an interact (in the PacketPlayerAttack listener before all checks).
- The real time reach check (which doesn't false because it doesn't check hitbox) runs on interact.
- The more accurate reach+hitbox check (which falses) runs on the next flying or transaction when this field is still true.
- Only after the flying/transaction has been processed by all packetChecks including Reach etc. (onPacketReceive in CheckManagerListener) we set it back to false

The field only has to be true for a single client tick, starting from the point we receive the interact, ending after we checked reach. Resetting it as early as possible is important (to not allow attack hitbox bypasses in the next tick). Once we receive a flying or a transaction, we can reset it safely because we know a new tick has started (this new tick can already have player influenced rotation again). Also, we're very certain to get a rotation packet directly after interacting with the horse because of the forced rotation change.

The single case where we don't receive a rotation but rather a transaction is in versions without the idle packet when the forced rotation change didn't actually modify the player's rotation (already oriented the same way as the horse!). Then we're at the beginning of the next tick and don't need to exempt anymore since the player could have already made some mouse input. If we need to exempt again the client will let us know by interacting with the horse again.

This is a rare thread issue/race condition as `Long2ObjectOpenhashMap` is not thread safe. We're using it store chunks for each player. This is a data structure we usually access on the player's netty thread however we call `isChunkLoaded` on the main bukkit thread (or respective region thread in folia).

There are few solutions we could try:
1. Make the map thread safe (minimal 2-3% performance hit, probably more; also possible to have staleness issues)
2. Make the Bukkit event scheduling running the `isChunkLoaded` check in the player's netty thread. (Performance hit from thread scheduling context switch and delay; has the very possible side effect of making our piston modeling even more desynced then it already is)
3. Finally get around to implementing piston support purely in packets (very difficult to do though hence the hacky Bukkit event workaround, has the bonus of meaning we won't have to re-implement this for other platforms)

### What **are** we storing – and *why does each layout work?* | # | Data we put on the wire | |---|-------------------------| | **1 (Current)**
`EncodedBlock` objects | • four **absolute** ints `x, y, z, blockId`.
• JVM object header for each block.

_Why it works:_ the full coordinates directly identify one block in the world. No packing, no shared state. | | **2 (4 ints)** | • Same four absolute ints as #1 but stored in **primitive arrays**, not objects.

_Why it works:_ still absolute coords, just cheaper because arrays have one header for many entries. | | **3 (Packed long + id)** | • Mojang’s **64-bit “section position”**: 22 b X-section, 22 b Z-section, 20 b Y-section (covers ±8 M blocks).
• Extra 12-bit “nibble” inside the packed value gives the **relative x/z/y **inside that 16³ section.
• Separate `int` for block-state id.

_Why it works:_ every block’s absolute coords can be reconstructed from: `(sectionX<<4)+relX`, `(sectionY<<4)+relY`, `(sectionZ<<4)+relZ`. This is literally what vanilla clients already do, so it is lossless. | | **4 (8-bit-Y long + id)** | • Same idea as #3 but we notice the game can only build from **Y = –64 … +319** by default and **-2031 to 2031** even with datapack modifications, the highest possible in vanilla.
• That is 24-254 vertical sections ⇒ fits in **8 bits** instead of Mojang’s 20.
• So we repack: 22 b X-sec, 22 b Z-sec, **8 b Y-sec**, plus 12-bit in-section nibble = 64 b total.
• Separate `int` id.

_Why it works:_ Y-section range –128…127 covers today’s default –4…+19 and even the max extended range with datapacks. If Mojang raises the ceiling again we still have ~100 spare section position values up to the datapack limit of -2031 to 2031 blocks. | | **5 (Section bucket: short + id)** | • One **64-bit header per section** (same 22/22/8 layout as #4).
• Then, for each block in that section:
  • one **12-bit** relative position stored in a `short` (0-4095).
  • one `int` block-state id.

_Why it works:_ the header already fixes the section coordinate, so every `short` only needs to say “which of the 4096 slots in this 16×16×16 box changed”. | | **6 (Bit-stream: 12-bit packed)** | • Same header as #5.
• First 12-bit position steals the 12 spare bits *inside* the header (no extra space).
• Remaining positions are written 12 bits at a time into a byte stream (1.5 B each).
• One parallel `int[]` for ids.

_Why it works:_ decoder reads the header, then pops 12-bit chunks until it reaches the number of ids. Saves another ~0.5 B per block over #5. | ### How the fixed overheads stack up * **Player-level (always live)** – one permanent runnable + its queue node ⇒ ~48 B (Options 2-6). * **Transaction buckets** (1 per transId) – 24 B for the object itself. * **Section buckets** (Opt-5 & 6 only) – 120–128 B for the three tiny objects plus two empty arrays. ### When does each option win? | Work-load | Best option | Why | |-----------|-------------|-----| | Very small packets (≤ 2 blocks) | **Opt 4** | No per-chunk key & 12 B/block beats 16 B ints | | Typical packets (3–100 blocks, single chunk) | **Opt 3** | 12 B/block + 8 B chunk key amortised | | Heavy redstone (hundreds of blocks across many sections) | **Opt 5** or **Opt 6** | Lower 6 B or 5.5 B/block outweigh section overhead at ~144+ updates/section | | Current code baseline | **Opt 1 (worst)** | 6–10 × more RAM & huge GC churn | ### Example – 10 000 updates, 400 sections, 1 transaction | Option | Live queue RAM | |--------|----------------| | 1 (current) | (80 B pkt + 36 B blk) ≈ **3.6 MB** | | 2 (4 ints) | 216 B bucket + 160 kB blocks ≈ **160 kB** | | 3 (chunk key) | 128 B bucket + 120 kB blocks ≈ **120 kB** | | 4 (8-bit Y) | 120 B bucket + 120 kB blocks ≈ **120 kB** | | 5 (short+int) | 24 B bucket + 400×120 B sections + 60 kB blocks ≈ **108 kB** | | 6 (bit-stream) | 24 B bucket + 400×128 B sections + 55 kB blocks ≈ **106 kB** | *Going from Option 1 to Option 5/6 cuts memory **~35×** and virtually eliminates young-gen GC churn.* --- ### Recommendation 1. Replace per-packet Runnables with **one** permanent runnable (Options 2-6). 2. Use **Option 3** if packets rarely cross chunk sections. 3. Use **Option 5** (or 6) if you expect hundreds of updates per section; Option 6 saves an extra 8 % RAM at the cost of slightly more bit-math. All options after `#1` are *dramatically* better than the current object-per-block approach in theory. ### RFC I'd like to hear from both users and other contributors their: 1. General Thoughts? 2. Did I make any obvious mistakes in my analysis? 3. How do you feel about the code complexity of some of the later options (don't worry about my ability to implement them, that's fine, I meant the maintainability of such a low level optimization)

I optimized handling multi block changes next. Here's what I have so far

Long-Array is basically equivalent to method 3, so there's more we can do. I haven't measured CPU usage yet but hopefully we should be able to break even or even gain performance through bypassing the PE wrapper and only checking the server version once to init a static field, which determines which version-specific handler for parsing multi block updates and adding runnables to use.

Theory seems to line up with practice. ~4x reduction as k -> infinity with some extra coming from reducing runnable overhead and Int array and long array perform the same when there is only 1 block in the multi block update.

| k (number of blocks in packet)  | Original (MB) | Low-Hanging (MB) | Int-Array (MB) | Long-Array (MB) |
|----|---------------|------------------|----------------|-----------------|
| 1  | 13.158 176 | 11.192 840 | 8.792 840 | 8.792 840 |
| 10 | 45.158 176 | 43.192 840 | 23.192 840 | 15.992 840 |
| 100| 369.158 176 | 367.192 840 | 167.192 840 | 87.992 840 |

You can find the code I used to get these numbers here: https://github.com/Axionize/LightningGrim/pull/new/optimize/block-updates-and-transaction-runnables although its a bit of a mess right now with lots of different benchmarks.

```
/**
 * Vanilla-only, tested against (≤ 1.21.4) multi-block-change handler that stores every
 * block record in ONE 32-bit int.
 *
 * Assumptions that make this possible
 * -----------------------------------
 *  • Vanilla has ~26 000 block states ⇒ 15 bits are enough.
 *  • A chunk-section is 16×16×16. Y-range –2031…2031 fits in 8 bits once
 *    you divide by 16 (shift right 4).
 *  • Server ≥ 1.20 ⇒ “trustEdges” byte disappeared from the packet.
 *
 * Layout we pack into the int   (MSB → LSB)
 * ┌───────────────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐
 * │ 31……17        │16…13 │12…9 │ 8…5 │ 4…0 │
 * │ blockStateId  │ lX   │ lZ  │ lY  │ free│
 * │   15 bits     │4 bits│4bits│4bits│5bits│
 * └───────────────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘
 * lX/lY/lZ  = 0-15 local coord in the section.
 * Five LSBs are currently unused but reserved for future flags.
 *
 * Section-position long (packet header)
 * ┌──────────22─────────┬──────────22─────────┬─────8────┬─1─┬──11─┐
 * │       secX          │       secZ          │  secY    │T? │free │
 * └─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┴──────────┴───┴─────┘
 * T? = old “trustEdges” flag (present only up to 1.19.4).
 * We leave 11 spare bits for mods / palette index, etc.
 */
```

Thought about this a little more and come up with a different bit repacking scheme that doesn't yet require reusing runnables like the other methods do (which means less structural refactoring).

#### So I added a millisecond delay option which was requested by a user (heckergato), the objective is to have a smoother command execution when multiple VLs are fired at once due to VL scaling. I also added an option which I will explain here:

---

TL;DR: The punishment system tracks how many times a command is executed (`executeCount`) for a given violation level (VL). The problem is: this counter never resets, not even when VL decays.

Example:
- You set a command to run at `20:20`.
- A player cheats, hits VL 20 → command runs.
- VL decays (player stops cheating for a bit).
- Player cheats again, hits VL 20 → **command does NOT run again**.

Why? Because the Grim thinks, “Ah, I already ran this command once for VL 20, no need to do it again.” Even though the VL dropped and came back up, which should be treated as a *new* violation threshold being reached.

Why This Sucks:
- **No repeat punishments or alerts**, even for repeated behaviour.
- **Mods might miss the first alert**, and the system gives them zero visibility after that.
- **Commands at specific VLs become useless** if they only ever fire once.
- Encourages a cheater to just chill for 5 minutes, then repeat the same thing forever without triggering anything again.

What Should Happen:
- `executeCount` should reset when VL decays past the previous threshold.

This is exactly what I have also implemented as a config option.

> what if the new rotation is still looking at the horse but is now out of range?

Ok I would have never thought of that. I tried it, and you're correct. There's still reach falses currently, the exact reproduction steps are:

- Spawn a horse with this command for 1.8 (other rotation values would work too but this makes it easy to test): `/summon EntityHorse ~ ~ ~ {Rotation:[25f,20f],NoAI:1}`
- Disable vehicle mounting using a plugin
- Right click the horse once to see the target rotation and don't move your mouse
- Walk away from the horse so far that you are still targeting the hitbox without reaching it with this rotation
- Stop walking before you can't reach the closest corner of its hitbox anymore
- Quickly aim from anywhere else (e.g. from above) and right click at the hitbox corner

The highest reach false I got during testing was 4.1 blocks.

As for the fix, I have simply moved the exemption I previously added slightly so that it also covers reach flags. However, when thinking it through I found that it would allow one bypass:

- Flag reach once so that the `cancelBuffer` is above zero
- Because of that, the simple realtime `getMinReachToBox` check in `isKnownInvalid` will not be executed anymore
- The precise check is now exempted for horses when interacting
- For a few hits, reach and hitbox would bypass on horses

To fix that, I execute the simple `getMinReachToBox` check again when exempting and use its result in place of the accurate check for horses. The simple check does not false as it always finds the optimal rotation.

What Grim version are you using? How are you running AntiCheatReplay they dropped support for us, unless you're using a modified version.

On a related note how important is AntiCheatReplay as a feature for you? I've been thinking about forking it to support Grim or make a PR but I don't see a lot of people using it.

I am using a dev version, 2.3.72-b88dfa7 because we tried with the latest stable release and the server didn't even start, for AntiCheatReplay we don't use it directly, we configured Grim to run a command to start a replay every time there is a violation, but it would be more convenient to have support for it out of the box. The feature of having replays was very very important, both for proving to the cheaters that they were cheating and also because if we weren't there we don't know if it was a false flag, I would love to see something implemented for it, maybe even in Grim so it just needs AdvancedReplay, and as a suggestion it would be nice to have a bit of recording before the flag happened, maybe it could start the recording when there is a violation and only save it if it detects cheating? And also it would be cool to see the violations in the replay chat to see at what exact moment it flagged what violations, also as general enhancements to Grim I think it is a really cool and really nice engine but I see it a bit lacking sometimes when it comes to the rest of things an AntiCheat does. I am not sure if this should maybe go on a separate repo with a name like "Grim+" (optional additions for Grim that are not included in the engine) but it would be really nice to see. For example, being able to check a player and at a glance seeing what are all their violations and how many they did (not a list of all violations but rather like `Simulation x2445 AntiKB x98` and so on one for each different check that has triggered and only showing each check once, not like history where it shows you each violation) *maybe on a GUI even?* Also some way of the alerts showing on a diff way and maybe even doing separate actions depending on how much it differs from the simulation and all of that, kind of like a `Confidence: High` where if the diff from the simulation is small it has a low confidence but if the diff is high it has a higher confidence, and for example with experimental checks it would have a lower confidence and for checks like reach it would have a very high confidence, also I think it would give more flexibility showing confidence as a percentage. Another thing I would really like is some kind of meta-analisys of the flags, some kind of heuristic engine that finds known patterns in the violations, for example if it triggers some `pre-flight` thing and then it triggers `ground spoof` and then it triggers `simulation` and it is more up than it should be, the meta-analisys could pick that up as flying, also the meta-analisys could have something like a player score, where it keeps track of their violations and it gets higher if they get many unrelated violations and especially if sometimes it gets a lot and sometimes a low amount or if it triggers things like heuristics... Basically instead of an alert when a violation triggers `x` amount of times on a short period of time an alert could be triggered by the "smarter" heuristics engine where it has in mind what violations happen, how much confidence, what order they have, if they follow a specific pattern (like flying), how much they differ from the simulation...

EDIT: This entire comment was wrong.

 The actual issue is that 1.8 servers have no configuration state, so the post-via listener is setting the decoder state to PLAY so the preVia listener is parsing CONFIGURATION packet as if they were play. This leads to the `SELECT_KNOWN_PACKS` packet on modern clients getting parsed as a `CHAT_COMMAND` packet.

Fixing this is rather difficult however because PE ties the Encoder/Decoder states to the `User` object which is shared between the preVia and postVIa listeners. Setting Configuration on PreVia on the previa listener will break decoding packets on the postVia listener...
You need to use our PacketEvents fork.

As a transcription: The linked video shows the player hitting the top of a shop NPC (player entity) on vanilla 1.8.9 Minecraft. There are two nametag lines above that shop NPC. The player is not aiming at the hitbox of the NPC itself, but rather at the labels. In chat, Grim alerts about Hitboxes, type=slime. So, this is not about the player entity.

I suspect that an outdated plugin on that server uses a slime entity with a zero or negative size to display the name tag. This was commonly used back in 1.7 when armor stands were not yet available for holograms. The issue can be reproduced on regular 1.8 Paper servers as well, for example with the following Bukkit plugin code:

```java
Location location = player.getEyeLocation()
Slime slime = (Slime) player.getWorld().spawnEntity(location, EntityType.SLIME);
slime.setSize(-1);
```

Once running this code, an inverted slime spawns at the player. Clicking around its hitbox will cause a false alert from Grim, so apparently the bounding box calculation we have implemented does not fully correspond to the vanilla one for slimes.

Most likely, this is not an issue with the bounding box calculation itself but with how the size is read from the entity metadata packets. In this part of Grim's code, the size is set to be at least 1, even though it could be 0 or negative:

Hey, sorry for the late reply.

I realized that I had been looking at the wrong method earlier.
I accidentally checked ``getOfflineFromUUID`` instead of ``getOfflineFromName``.

The CraftBukkit approach using ``UUID.nameUUIDFromBytes(("OfflinePlayer:" + name))`` is actually a nice solution.
But the ``getProfileByName`` call was taking several seconds on my server before it finally failed.

My question is: why should we perform an extra Mojang profile lookup when we can store this information?
That way we're not dependent on Mojang being online.

So my idea is basically, we should only display data that has been loaded at least once already.
If the database has never seen that player before the result for the history will always be empty.

The Mojang lookup currently only happens when the server doesn't already know the player.
This mostly occurs on setups like minigame networks or multi server environments (e.g. citybuild + farmworld), where player data isn't synchronized between servers.

And storing the data centrally in a database, rather than on each individual server by fetching a GameProfile with textures and other metadata, is a better approach. I think.

Did you benchmark the custom queue to make sure it was really faster than ArrayDeque? In most cases we are removing from the head, not the middle. Since ArrayDeque is implemented as a ring buffer, removal from the head is O(1). When you factor in the additional GC pressure from the Node allocations in a Linked List, I'd be very surprised if it was actually faster.

I did some experimenting a long time ago when I was optimizing block update runnables with changing the LatencyUtil impl as well. You can find my old experiments and JMH code here https://github.com/Axionize/LightningGrim/tree/optimize/block-updates-and-transaction-runnables if you would like to test.

> I don't think it's necessary to keep the order of async and netty transactions, if so, would blocking netty thread for a while and server tick thread still running, breaks the plugin? The order of this two is never certain, and I'm really not a fan of making everything "right"; I want everything to be "fit" and efficient. I don't like to add any uncessary concurrent cost on netty thread.

It sounds ridiculous, right? I was just as astonished when I discovered this when I started working on Grim. But yes, in the current implementation, if you block the netty or main thread, updates will be applied out of order and can cause falses.

Since we only use the async tasks for handling pistons its fine, this is fairly rare. For best chance of reproduction you gotta be colliding with pistons (especially with slime or honey blocks) and other blocks. While I've wanted to replace it for a long time, its one of those things that's really difficult to do and the current solution is "good enough" (people don't get stuck on slimeblock launchers, and it's not like PVP maps are made of moving slime block platforms... although now that I think about it, that sounds fun).

The issue is that while the current code is technically incorrect (race condition), your proposed changes are "more incorrect" because they ensure updates will *always* be applied out of order in those scenarios.

> This patch works perfectly fine in my production environment. If you insist on getting the most perfect implementation directly, I would close this PR.

I'm sorry if I've come across as combative. I don't need the "most perfect" implementation, but I do need to ensure there are no correctness regressions.

I have plenty of times pushed out an update I've tested that I thought was falseless, only to have issues start trickling in as soon as it hit the tens of thousands of servers that run Grim. May I ask what kind of server you've run this on in prod?

If you want, I can test out some variations of this in [LightningGrim](https://modrinth.com/plugin/lightning-grim-anticheat), similar to my block update runnable optimizations. If they prove stable, I can merge them upstream. I usually route all our experimental changes that way, as it has a fairly large user base for reporting issues who understand that it's experimental.

I understand this can feel frustrating for what seems like such a simple PR, but when you touch something as core as LatencyUtils and change execution order we need to ensure its correct and that takes a lot of data from tons of servers in production and time.

All my changes are based on performance analysis tools in my production environment. This is a Folia server with over 50 players and many farms/mob farms.
  
  I started the change when I occasionally noticed the synchronized block took ~4% of my CPU on netty thread. This race isn't even a persistence issue – I frequently do performance analysis to uncover potential problems on the server. I have reason to believe this is caused by a subset of players (most likely using pistons). Only a small number of players can cause so much overhead. What if more players were in this kind of extreme environment?
  
  Like my commit time, I used ArrayDeque and runs it on my production environment. This yielded a stable 3% occupancy, it was moving elements. The problem is that some transaction is added in player.lastTransactionSent, some are lastTransactionSent + 1. It's not all at head in order. So we have the cost.
  
  World changes on the tick thread are not updated just in time. They are deferred until a certain time before being sent to the player from the queue. This sync system is made in magic and lacks reliability already.
  
  Finally, this PR became what it is now. I've observed it for a long time and no longer see the queue processing causing a significant overhead. It's just 0.0%.

 I understand the reliability concerns, but I also have performance concerns. Grim is such a low-level plugin that core performance is extremely important. Perhaps in the first place, asynchronous transactions should not appear, but rather packets should have been used instead.

I need to clarify – because world changes on the tick thread are not in time, in the current live build, piston changes are always either ahead of time or sync between all transactions.

However, the modified queue impl may be ahead, or delayed, or sync.

Regardless of the modification, this prediction is inaccurate. This PR is unlikely to change or amplify the problem, because inconsistency already exists... Unless we move to packet based pistion movements, but I have no interest in doing it.

Ok, let me write on an update on the current situation because this ended up being far more complicated than I thought and this may take some time to deal with in 2.0.

We currently use the attributes of the Itemstack in hand at the time of attack to calculate Reach. Reach being attribute swappable means we have to do a lot of work to model the client-side state of this instead, this alone wouldn't be insurmountable just difficult in 2.0's architecture.

However:
1. Paper makes attribute swapping being disabled the default, however for spears (and other items that change Reach distance) its completely broken. When swapping from the spear to another weapon `unsupported-settings.update-equipment-on-player-action: true` does not work and you can land hits with the reach of the spear and the base damage of the 2nd weapon.
2. The Fabric mod fixes this correctly, and will allow the hit to go through but with the damage of the spear: https://modrinth.com/mod/attribute-swapping-fix (although its slightly inefficient in that it sends one more packet than strictly necessary)

This means patching this would mean allowing attribute swapping on Paper servers that have it disabled, which is the vast majority of them. Effectively I am in the unenviable position of waiting on Paper to make or merge in a PR by me to fix an unsupported setting (which probably isn't high on their priority list), or to allow attribute swapping on servers that don't want it.

Considering that this affects all Paper servers regardless of the config, would it not be an option to assume that reach attribute swapping is enabled until it is resolved?

Also, how would the functionality of a check determine whether attribute swapping is enabled on servers? Wouldn't this be handled separately through server code instead? For example, if the server handled it similar to the mod (where the attributes of the spear are used), that does not change whether the hit was possible in terms of reach/hitboxes. In fact it would be handled the same as assuming that reach attribute swapping is allowed.

(Just a sidenote, the reason the option does not work seems to be due to the attributes of the 2nd item always being prioritized, which works in most cases. However the reach attribute is a special case where the only feasible way to patch this would be do to the reverse instead, which is what the mod seems to do)

​To answer your question: the current regex actually breaks the proxy support intended in #734 because it strictly hardcodes https://discord.com. The regex in #734 was much looser ((?:https?://)?(?:\w+\.)?\w+\.\w+/api...) and allowed different domains.

​Regarding the URL pattern: while standard proxies might keep the /api/webhooks/... path structure, custom middleware solutions—such as routing through a Matrix bot (e.g., Maubot plugins)—use completely different domains and path structures that do not match the official Discord API pattern at all.

​To provide a bit of context on why this is needed: in regions with strict network environments, accessing the Discord API directly is highly unstable and cumbersome. Meanwhile, local alternative platforms often strictly restrict or forbid bot usage. Therefore, routing traffic through custom self-hosted middleware or Matrix forwarders is often our most practical workaround.

​Because of these edge cases, the best approach would be to keep the current verification to prevent standard users from making typos, but add a configuration toggle (e.g., disable-webhook-validation: true defaulting to false). This allows advanced users to bypass the regex check entirely and input any valid HTTP/HTTPS endpoint for their custom setups, without you having to maintain an overly complex regex.

​We really appreciate your understanding in accommodating these unique networking constraints!

@Axionize The main problem is that MySQL doesn't have a native UUID type, whereas PostgreSQL does. Therefore, there is no clean solution to handle it at the database level, because depending on the chosen database, there is always some manual mapping needed. A workaround could be to create a `getUuid` method in the `DatabaseDialect` interface and pass the dialect into every method where the UUID is needed. Or the SQL stuff could be rewritten to use an ORM like [Querydsl](https://www.baeldung.com/intro-to-querydsl#QueryDSL), but both approaches mean a lot of changes, and if I remember correctly, you yourself [said](https://discord.com/channels/811396969670901800/1490491850736275648/1490779052980699227) that this system is going to get rebuilt in a few months.

Well it's been a while since I did all this, and I mostly figured it out through trial and error. The problem was that when using one of the existing sprinting variables, it would always false either when you start sprinting, or when you stop sprinting (due to an attack). At first I wanted to use a different sprinting state for when you're attacking, but it's of course a bad solution and didn't quite work. So eventually I figured it probably has nothing to do with attacking, but rather just the server stopping your sprint, which seems to behave differently than any other sprint state change for some reason. That's why when the server stops the sprint, it's slightly delayed until it actually counts as stopped.
If it fixes issues, it's fine. Fixing packet sprinting likely requires more in depth work for 2.0, although I have a solid understanding of how sprinting works, but that's for another day to fix.

I appreciate the feedback! However, this check is fundamentally different from a standard KeepSprint check. While KeepSprint looks for the lack of slowdown, AttackMomentum specifically targets unnatural velocity consistency (precision) during combat.

Regarding the 'ideal conditions' concern: the check is actually more robust because of them. Since it only flags when the velocity difference is extremely low (near zero), any environmental factor like hitting a block, speed attribute changes, or even micro-fluctuations in movement would cause the velocity to change, which would naturally prevent a flag.

It's specifically designed to catch sophisticated clients that 'lock' their momentum to a perfectly constant value to stay just under the threshold of other movement checks while attacking. It's about catching the 'perfect' precision that a human or normal game physics wouldn't produce.
These values target the artificial precision of ghost clients, and I've used a 4-tick buffer to prevent false positives from brief, natural physics quirks.

@Axionize Yep! I am unable to false the check by attribute swapping now. The extra verbose flags are very helpful, thank you. However, I found another (related but different) false that only involves items with a `hitbox_margin` set. I mentioned before that there is an additional range check made if there is no attribute swapping done. I will refer to this method as the same as the src: `isInRange`. However, due to the geometry of Mojang's implementation of `hitbox_margin`, this method can actually pass with the extra movement reach added. `ProjectileUtil#getManyEntityHitResult()` handles hitbox margins by expanding the AABB by the margin, then performing another raycast to the centre of the hitbox onto the non-expanded AABB. The hit result location is on this non-expanded box, **not** the expanded box. This might be hard to visualize, so I included a rough sketch demonstrating an item with `max_reach: 5.0` and `hitbox_margin: 0.5`. It assumes an extra movement value of `0.01`. The top vector with length `x` is the one that `isInRange` would check the length of. Here's the problem: `isInRange` effectively checks for whether the distance between the eye and the hit result is under `max_reach + hitbox_margin`. In this example, it would check for a maximum value of `5.5`. However, we can see that the actual vector it is checking for will only be ~5.5 if the player is looking directly at the centre of the entity's hitbox. It is shorter in all other cases. So, when the extra movement value is included, even if the actual reach to the expanded AABB is >5.00, `isInRange` will allow the hit to go through since the vector it is checking for will almost always be less than 5.5. Note that this does not affect spears anymore since the only way to attack using this is through attribute swapping, which is handled. I might've butchered this explanation, so let me know if I need to clarify. --- If you want to keep this separate from the original attribute swapping false, I can make a separate issue with these details.

Player connecting → PacketType.Play.Server.JOIN_GAME → player is teleported to the new world → PacketType.Play.Server.RESPAWN → CHUNK_DATA packets for the new world are sent.

The problem is that player.compensatedWorld.chunks.clear() is executed inside player.addRealTimeTaskNext(() -> {}). Because of that, some of the CHUNK_DATA packets are processed before the chunks.clear() call actually runs. As a result, those chunks are added to the compensated world and then immediately removed when chunks.clear() is finally executed.

Alright. If my explanation wasn't clear enough, I've prepared a detailed debug log using the latest version of GrimAC without any modifications other than the debug output itself.

I tested this on two different server implementations: SSSPigot and Paper build 794 (MC 1.16.5).

I understand that reproducing this issue may depend on several factors, such as CPU speed, the exact vanilla packet ordering, or network latency.

### 1. SSSPigot 1.16.5

Tested on a VPS with an AMD Ryzen 9 5950X.

https://pastes.dev/OQVgfdmdL8

The setup uses two normal worlds.

As you can see, after the player joins, two chunks from World 1 are received (`15,1` and `14,1`). After that, only chunks from World 2 are received. Interestingly, some of those World 2 chunk packets even arrive before `JOIN_GAME`/`RESPAWN`.

On line 17 you can see that execution reaches `player.addRealTimeTaskNext()` while handling the `RESPAWN` packet.

However, the player's current chunk (`0,0`) had already been processed long before that.

On line 44, `chunks.clear()` is finally executed, which removes chunk `(0,0)` from the compensated world.

After that, there are repeated `insideUnloadedChunk (chunk=0,0 column=null)` debug messages confirming that the chunk is no longer present.

The end result is that the player cannot move because Grim believes they are inside an unloaded chunk.

### 2. Paper build 794

Tested on a residential "potato" server.

https://pastes.dev/o7KUls0v9Q

In this setup, the first world is the normal overworld and the second world is the Nether.

The behavior is very similar to the first test.

P.S. I'm not claiming this bug is guaranteed to reproduce in every environment. In my production server it happened for every first-time player joining the server, which is why I started investigating it.

Based on everything I've observed, I do believe this is a real issue, and I think it should be fixed properly in Grim rather than worked around externally.

Fixed in GrimAnticheat/GrimAPI#34 / GrimAPI 1.6.0.9, picked up by Grim `2.0` in 41b8b61e4 — the fix will be in the next build after 2.3.74.

**Root cause:** databases created by Grim builds from roughly late April to mid-May store violation ids as `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`. Newer builds write UUIDv7 ids, and the storage cutover in June stopped running the migration that converted that column — so on upgraded databases every violation write failed with `SQLITE_MISMATCH` and spammed the console. Fresh databases were unaffected.

**What to do:** nothing — on first startup with the fixed build the table is rebuilt automatically (existing violation history is preserved; old numeric ids become time-ordered UUIDv7s). @linsaftw you can re-enable the database once you're on that build.

I looked into how Paper actually handles dotted keys, to see if Grim needs to deal with them at all. Refs against PaperMC/Paper@26e81c450

Turns out it depends on the file.

spigot.yml goes through Bukkit's YamlConfiguration, which gets saved back on startup (SpigotConfig.java:49,99). The flattening happens on load, fromNodeTree (YamlConfiguration.java:150) hands the literal key to MemorySection#createSection/#set (MemorySection.java:281,190), and both split on "." (ConfigurationOptions.java:10). createSection handles your flat-parent case, set the flat-leaf one. So the file is already nested by the time Grim opens it.

config/paper-global.yml is the opposite. It uses Configurate (PaperConfigurations.java:77-84), where dots aren't separators at all. The flat key is just unrecognised, the default kicks in, and Velocity stays off. No warning, the stray key stays in the file.

So the flat-key handling wasn't buying anything, where the format works Paper already converted it, and where it doesn't the proxy really is off. Removed it

This is not specific to SSSPigot, and it is not really about packet arrival order either. The race is between two latency tasks that are never ordered against each other.

`addToCache` schedules the insert at the transaction current when the chunk packet was read:

https://github.com/GrimAnticheat/Grim/blob/2.0/common/src/main/java/ac/grim/grimac/utils/latency/CompensatedWorld.java#L659-L663

The respawn handler clears the whole map from `addRealTimeTaskNext`, i.e. one transaction later. When the server sends the new world's chunks before the respawn's trailing transaction has been written, those chunk tasks land on the *earlier* transaction and therefore run first. The clear then wipes chunks that have already been delivered and that the server will never send again, because from its point of view the client has them.

From there `insideUnloadedChunk()` is true forever, so `MovementCheckRunner` force-resyncs every movement packet, waiting for a chunk that already arrived. Hence the loop. The comment on that path even says "Keep re-teleporting until they load the chunk!" — which is exactly the assumption that breaks here.

Whether it reproduces depends on how fast the server gets those chunk packets out relative to the transaction write, which is why it looks fork- and hardware-dependent. The defect is present regardless.

### A fix that does not depend on task ordering

Rather than trying to order the two tasks, make the outcome independent of which runs first. Stamp each `Column` with a world generation, incremented **synchronously while handling the respawn packet** — packet order is real ordering, unlike task order:

- every column read after that respawn is stamped with the new generation;
- the respawn's deferred cleanup removes only columns belonging to worlds the player has left, instead of clearing the map;
- a column whose task is still pending when its world is superseded is dropped on insert rather than resurrecting itself.

Either execution order then produces the correct result. We have been running this on a fork for a few days without falses.

Worth noting that the same block clears `entityMap`, `activePistons` and `openShulkerBoxes`, and entity spawns are deferred the same way, so the identical race exists for entities. That one is quieter and arguably worse — a wiped entity is simply invisible to every check that looks it up, with no loop to make it obvious. Filed separately.

Confirmed, and the cause is a sampling point rather than the reset itself.

Vanilla compares the main hand item **once per tick**, in `Player.tick()`, against the item held at the end of the previous tick, and resets the attack strength ticker only when the item type actually differs. Both the client and the server run that comparison there, so they always agree.

`AttackCooldownHandler` samples per packet instead: `updateHeldItem()` is called from the inventory whenever the selected slot changes, not only from the tick branch. A client that switches away and back inside a single tick therefore sends two packets that each look like a change to Grim and reset the cooldown twice, while neither the client nor the server resets theirs. That is the whole disabler.

`getMinimumProgress()` then falls under the 0.9 gate in `PacketPlayerAttack`, `minAttackSlow` is never raised, and the prediction engine stops requiring the attacker to slow down — so keeping sprint is accepted.

### Fix

Do the comparison only on the tick packet, and remove the out-of-band calls that trigger it mid-tick. The `stackChanged` field exists solely to compensate for those calls (it skips the increment when a reset already happened out of band) and goes away with them.

This also corrects the opposite skew, which is a real if less interesting bug: a player who drew a weapon and attacked in the same tick previously had the cooldown reset *before* the attack was judged, so a legitimate full-strength hit was treated as not-yet-charged. Vanilla never does that either, because the comparison happens after the attack in the tick.

Adapting the disabler to switch once per tick would no longer help: the client and the server both reset in that case too, so the states stay in agreement, which is the definition of not a bypass.

Correcting myself: the main claim above is wrong, and I should have checked before filing.

I wrote that punishment thresholds built on these violations end up firing on how long a player has been online. They do not. `PunishmentManager` keeps its own time-limited list and compares thresholds against `group.violations.size()`, with entries expiring after `remove-violations-after` (default 300s). `check.violations` reaches it only as the `%vl%` placeholder in the alert text.

I also assumed the monotonic value fed setbacks through `violations > setbackVL`. It does not for these two: `Reach` and `Hitboxes` flag with `flag(...)` and never go through `setbackIfAboveSetbackVL()`, so `setbackVL` is inert for them.

So the absence of `reward()` has no enforcement consequence at all. What is left is narrower and only about readability: the VL shown in an alert is a lifetime count rather than a recent measure, which is inconsistent with the checks that do reward, and it is genuinely misleading to read. It misled me - I took a VL of 22600 in our logs as a severity signal when it was just a long-running total of false positives from a separate ported check, and the real problem was that check's false positives.

Whether that is worth changing is a judgement call I am not well placed to make from outside. Feel free to close this; I would rather withdraw an incorrect report than leave it standing.

That premise was mine, not the reporter's, and if PacketEvents guarantees the post-send task runs before any further write on that channel then my description is simply wrong. One thing I would still flag, because it cuts the other way from how the bracketing is usually described as the defence here. Walking the numbering:

- handling RESPAWN calls `sendTransaction()`, so `lastTransactionSent` is now n+1;
- `addRealTimeTaskNext` therefore schedules the clear at n+2;
- a chunk read at any point before the trailing transaction is written carries n+1, so its task runs at n+1 - strictly *before* the clear.

So the leading transaction does not protect against this. It shifts both numbers by one and leaves the clear scheduled strictly later than any chunk read before the trailing write. What protects against it is only the write-ordering guarantee itself. If that guarantee holds, there is no bug and nothing to do; if it is ever violated by a platform or a fork, the bracketing will not catch it.

That is the only reason I'd still argue for a stamp over an ordering assumption: it makes the outcome independent of the guarantee rather than dependent on it. Not pressing the point - your call entirely, and if the answer is "packetevents guarantees this, fix packetevents", that closes it cleanly.

You're right, and thanks - that kills the fix as I described it. Tick packets are not a reliable per-tick signal on those versions, so the comparison can arrive late, and a player who genuinely switches weapons and attacks before the next one would be judged with a cooldown that has not been reset. That is a false positive in the opposite direction from the bypass, which is worse than the bypass.

What survives is separating *where the comparison is made against* from *when it is evaluated*. Keep a snapshot of the item as of the last observed tick boundary, and evaluate against it in two places: on the tick packet as before, and again at attack time, without moving the snapshot.

- switch away and back inside one tick, then attack: current item equals the snapshot, nothing resets - the disabler stops working;
- genuine switch, then attack, with no tick packet in between: current item differs from the snapshot, it resets there and then - no dependency on a tick packet arriving.

The snapshot staying put across the attack-time evaluation is the whole trick; moving it would reintroduce the per-packet behaviour.

That leaves `ticksSinceLastSwing` itself, which is incremented on tick packets and so already undercounts across skipped ticks - but that is existing behaviour, unchanged by any of this, and presumably handled by whatever compensates for tick skipping elsewhere. If it is not, the cooldown is understated on those versions for reasons that have nothing to do with slot switching.
